classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of four numerical arguments into a supplied quadratic rule.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly evaluates the supplied function at a numerical argument; function-notation is the closest directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Substitute each input into the rule, evaluate powers first, then simplify. Example 1 on PDF page 3 demonstrates numerical substitution, including parentheses around a negative argument.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of four numerical arguments into a supplied quadratic rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct numerical substitution into a supplied quadratic rule, including negative inputs.

questions.mappingNote: Each part evaluates a supplied function at a numerical input; function-notation is the closest catalogue skill. The numerical substitution method in Example 1 applies directly.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 introduces function rules and input-output values. Example 1 on page 3 substitutes numerical inputs into a quadratic rule, evaluates powers and simplifies, retaining parentheses around negative inputs. Page 4 extends substitution to algebraic expressions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct numerical substitution into a supplied quadratic rule, including negative inputs.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of three numerical inputs into each of four supplied function rules.

questions.mappingNote: Each part evaluates the same three numerical inputs in a supplied rule. Function notation is the closest directly assessed skill, including the exponential rule in part d.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 introduces a function rule and input/output variables. Page 3, Example 1, substitutes numerical inputs, brackets negative inputs and evaluates powers before arithmetic. Page 4, Example 3, reinforces replacement of the complete argument in a function rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of three numerical inputs into each of four supplied function rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of three numerical inputs into linear, reciprocal, quadratic and square-root function rules.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly evaluate h at the same three numerical inputs; function-notation is the closest supplied skill, including for the reciprocal and square-root rules.
questions.methodNote: Function notation associates each input with its output. Example 1 substitutes numerical inputs into the rule, uses parentheses around negative inputs, and evaluates powers before completing the arithmetic. Example 3 reinforces replacing every occurrence of the argument.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of three numerical inputs into linear, reciprocal, quadratic and square-root function rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Replace the input variable consistently in three explicitly supplied function rules.

questions.mappingNote: Each part applies that substitution method with the argument t. No expansion or numerical evaluation is required.
questions.methodNote: Function notation identifies the input; Example 3 replaces every occurrence of x with the specified algebraic argument.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Replace the input variable consistently in three explicitly supplied function rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Repeated direct substitution of small integers into quadratic and cubic rules, recording each output in its supplied table.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess direct evaluation of function rules at specified numerical inputs. Function notation is the closest catalogue skill; graph construction is not requested.
questions.methodNote: Use the input–output rule and substitute each listed input. Page 3 Example 1 demonstrates numerical substitution, including negative inputs; Example 2 records calculated outputs in a value table.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Repeated direct substitution of small integers into quadratic and cubic rules, recording each output in its supplied table.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate a linear function at specified inputs, then combine its outputs using subtraction, multiplication, addition and division.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess evaluation in function notation followed by arithmetic on outputs; function-notation is the closest existing skill.
questions.methodNote: Substitute each input into the function rule, evaluate its output, then perform the indicated arithmetic. Page 3 Example 1 demonstrates numerical substitution and brackets around negative inputs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate a linear function at specified inputs, then combine its outputs using subtraction, multiplication, addition and division.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the order-sensitive verbal rule into function notation, then substitute five signed inputs.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 directly combines the verbal-rule and numerical-substitution methods from page 3; function-notation is the closest directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 introduces function rules and value tables. Page 3 Example 2 translates a verbal rule into an equation and a value table; Example 1 substitutes signed inputs with parentheses. Page 4 extends substitution to algebraic inputs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate the order-sensitive verbal rule into function notation, then substitute five signed inputs.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute binomial surd inputs into a quadratic, expand the squares and collect exact terms.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts evaluate a quadratic at a compound surd argument, directly applying the substitution-and-expansion method of Example 3. The supplied reuse candidates have different givens and assessed tasks.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the complete input in brackets, expand its square, then collect terms. Page 3 Example 1 demonstrates numerical substitution; page 4 Example 3 demonstrates substitution and expansion of compound arguments.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute binomial surd inputs into a quadratic, expand the squares and collect exact terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the required dependent variable and rearrange linear, reciprocal, square and cube formulas, choosing the positive square root for a physical length.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10 assesses expressing a rule with a specified independent or dependent variable. Function notation is the closest catalogue skill; linear rearrangement supports parts a and b. The supplied teaching does not contain a worked rearrangement example, so ordinary prerequisite algebra supplies those steps.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 distinguishes independent inputs from dependent outputs. Page 3 expresses function rules as equations. Page 4 requires natural restrictions arising from practical situations. Make the requested dependent variable the subject using inverse operations; take the positive square root for a length.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the required dependent variable and rearrange linear, reciprocal, square and cube formulas, choosing the positive square root for a physical length.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine a fixed cover fee with a constant cost per person to write one linear function.

questions.mappingNote: Replace the fixed fee and per-item charge with the restaurant's cover fee and charge per person. The directly assessed skill is modelling a real-life linear relationship.
questions.methodNote: The electrician example combines a fixed fee with a charge per item as y=100+40x; the following page expresses the same rule using function notation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine a fixed cover fee with a constant cost per person to write one linear function.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute each input and explain the resulting restriction, distinguishing negative radicands from zero denominators.

questions.mappingNote: Each part substitutes the specified input and identifies why the resulting expression has no real value. Natural-domain-from-equation is the closest skill because negative radicands and zero denominators are the assessed restrictions.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines a function as a rule with possible restrictions. Page 3 Example 1 demonstrates numerical substitution. Page 4 discusses restrictions and includes square-root and reciprocal functions in the exercise.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute each input and explain the resulting restriction, distinguishing negative radicands from zero denominators.

classification.difficultyReason: Substituting three algebraic arguments requires sign handling, binomial expansion and simplification of reciprocal expressions.

questions.mappingNote: Each part evaluates the same rule at a, -a and a+1; algebraic-argument evaluation is the directly assessed skill, including the reciprocal rule in part d.
questions.methodNote: Replace every occurrence of the input variable with the complete argument in parentheses, then simplify. Page 4 Example 3 demonstrates algebraic substitution and binomial expansion.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substituting three algebraic arguments requires sign handling, binomial expansion and simplification of reciprocal expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish subtracting 2 from the output from substituting t−2 as the input, then expand and simplify quadratic expressions.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses substitution of t−2 into a function and distinguishes this from subtracting 2 from F(t); algebraic-argument evaluation is the closest and most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the input–output interpretation and function notation from pages 2–3. Follow Example 3 on page 4: substitute the entire algebraic argument in parentheses, expand, and simplify.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguish subtracting 2 from the output from substituting t−2 as the input, then expand and simplify quadratic expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute algebraic arguments into a quadratic, expand and factor the resulting numerators to simplify three difference quotients.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses evaluation at algebraic arguments followed by simplification; no limit or differentiation is requested.
questions.methodNote: Use function notation to substitute the complete input expression, then expand brackets and simplify as demonstrated in Example 3 on PDF page 4. Factor the difference-quotient numerator before cancelling its nonzero denominator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute algebraic arguments into a quadratic, expand and factor the resulting numerators to simplify three difference quotients.

classification.difficultyReason: Verify three identities by algebraic substitution, handling negative powers and simplifying a compound rational expression.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts assess substitution of an algebraic argument and simplification to verify a specified identity. Parts a and b also exhibit the even/odd tests, but part c is a reciprocal-argument identity.
questions.methodNote: Use function notation and direct substitution, as demonstrated by Example 1 on PDF page 3 and algebraic substitution in Example 3 on PDF page 4. Simplify powers and fractions while retaining the stated restrictions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Verify three identities by algebraic substitution, handling negative powers and simplifying a compound rational expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate a function with the input in both its base and exponent, then interpret the numerical trend.

questions.mappingNote: The question assesses numerical evaluation in function notation and an observation from the resulting outputs; no formal limit calculation is required.
questions.methodNote: Substitute each input into every occurrence of the variable in the function rule, following Example 1, and evaluate using a calculator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate a function with the input in both its base and exponent, then interpret the numerical trend.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the two supplied rules, expand their squares, cancel matching terms and apply the index product law.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is an algebraic identity involving defined functions; expansion and simplification are the most advanced directly assessed operations.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the function rules, expand and simplify algebraically, following the substitution and expansion approach of Example 3 on PDF page 4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute the two supplied rules, expand their squares, cancel matching terms and apply the index product law.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the vertical line test to six supplied graphs and illustrate a repeated input.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed skill is recognising relations that fail the one-output-per-input condition through the vertical line test.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 Example 7 identifies two points with the same x-coordinate and joins them with a vertical line. Page 11 states that one vertical line meeting a relation more than once proves it is not a function. Apply this directly to the six supplied graphs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the vertical line test to six supplied graphs and illustrate a repeated input.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the named vertical line test to the solid curves, then read their horizontal and vertical extents from turning points, filled endpoints and arrows.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts assess graphical recognition of a function by the vertical line test; the supplied graphs need no algebraic manipulation or domain calculation.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 defines a function by unique output for each input. Page 10 Example 7 demonstrates two points with the same x-coordinate. Page 11 Key Idea 8 states the vertical line test: one vertical line meeting a relation more than once disproves that it is a function.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the vertical line test to eight supplied graphs, distinguishing a relation from its dashed construction guide.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate two familiar functions, plot their tabulated points and read the domain and range of the complete curves.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess completing tables and sketching quadratic or exponential functions, followed by graph-based domain and range. The table's finite sample inputs do not restrict either function's domain.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 evaluates a function in a value table, forms ordered pairs and joins plotted points with a smooth curve. Pages 8–9 define domain and range and read them graphically; page 9 explicitly uses the natural domain when no restriction is stated. Page 11 uses 2^x as a function example.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate two familiar functions, plot their tabulated points and read the domain and range of the complete curves.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the stated restriction on division by zero to three linear denominators.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess finding a natural domain algebraically by excluding a zero denominator.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines the natural domain as all valid real inputs. Example 6(a) excludes a zero denominator by writing x−2≠0 and hence x≠2. Apply that same method to each denominator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the stated restriction on division by zero to three linear denominators.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly supplied square-root restriction to three radicands, requiring at most one linear rearrangement.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts request natural domains directly from square-root equations. The natural-domain skill covers the assessed task; square-root validity is the supporting condition.
questions.methodNote: PDF page 9 defines the natural domain as all valid inputs and states that square roots of negative numbers are undefined. Example 6(b) requires x−2≥0 and rearranges to x≥2. Apply that same radicand restriction in each part.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly supplied square-root restriction to three radicands, requiring at most one linear rearrangement.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the one-output-per-input definition directly to four finite mapping diagrams and justify each classification.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts ask whether a finite relation is a function and require reasons. Checking outgoing arrows and identifying a repeated input with distinct outputs directly assesses relations-and-functions.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 defines a function by the requirement that no input has two outputs. Pages 10–11 distinguish general relations from functions using repeated inputs with different outputs; Example 8 demonstrates classification with an explicit counterexample.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the one-output-per-input definition directly to four finite mapping diagrams and justify each classification.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly read two labelled points with a common x-coordinate from each supplied graph; the required criterion is explicitly given.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts identify the defining failure of a function through ordered pairs, so relations-and-functions is the closest directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 Example 7 selects two graph points with the same x-coordinate and different outputs. Page 11 states the vertical line test. Apply this graphical method directly without requiring equations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly read two labelled points with a common x-coordinate from each supplied graph; the required criterion is explicitly given.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the relevant domain restriction for each formula, combining non-negative radicands with non-zero denominators in parts e and f.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 asks for natural domains directly from six formulas. Parts a–d use unrestricted linear expressions, non-zero denominators or non-negative radicands; parts e–f combine both restrictions. The natural-domain-from-equation skill directly covers all six.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines natural domain as all valid real inputs. Its two restrictions exclude zero denominators and negative radicands. Example 6 applies these restrictions algebraically; page 12 question 5 and page 13 question 6 provide immediate practice with each restriction separately.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select the relevant domain restriction for each formula, combining non-negative radicands with non-zero denominators in parts e and f.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect the square-root domain, rounded table values and a smooth graph, then recognise the curve as half a sideways parabola.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10 combines the natural domain of a square-root rule with calculator table values, graph construction and recognition of the square-root curve. Graph-square-root-function is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 demonstrates substitution into a value table, plotting ordered pairs and joining them with a smooth curve. Page 9 defines natural domain and requires non-negative radicands. Page 10 illustrates the sideways parabola y²=x, supporting recognition of its upper half.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect the square-root domain, rounded table values and a smooth graph, then recognise the curve as half a sideways parabola.

classification.difficultyReason: Exclude the undefined input, evaluate positive and negative fractional inputs, and use the table to construct two disconnected hyperbola branches.

questions.mappingNote: Graph-inverse-variation is the closest catalogue match for the main construction y=2/x. Domain exclusion and function evaluation support parts a and b. The solution follows the requested table-and-plot method.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 demonstrates substitution into a value table, plotting ordered pairs and joining a smooth curve. Page 9 defines the natural domain and excludes zero denominators in Example 6a. Question 11 supplies the name rectangular hyperbola and directs a two-part curve.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Exclude the undefined input, evaluate positive and negative fractional inputs, and use the table to construct two disconnected hyperbola branches.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive a quadratic area rule from a fixed perimeter, restrict its domain using positive side lengths, and sketch the restricted parabola.

questions.mappingNote: Domain restriction is directly assessed alongside constructing an area function and its graph; domain-and-range is the closest supplied skill covering the complete task.
questions.methodNote: Pages 7–8 model a contextual quadratic, restrict the input using the physical situation, and distinguish included and excluded endpoints. Use positive rectangle side lengths and sketch the resulting restricted parabola.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derive a quadratic area rule from a fixed perimeter, restrict its domain using positive side lengths, and sketch the restricted parabola.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange linear and rational relations, apply square-root and denominator restrictions, and explain why each valid input determines one output.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts ask for a single-valued output rule and justification that it is a function; natural-domain restrictions support the rational and square-root cases.
questions.methodNote: Use the one-output-per-input definition on page 7 and the natural-domain restrictions on page 9: exclude zero denominators and negative radicands. Interpret square-root notation as the principal nonnegative root.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange linear and rational relations, apply square-root and denominator restrictions, and explain why each valid input determines one output.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine denominator restrictions with square-root conditions, factor quadratics and distinguish strict from inclusive endpoints.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses the natural domain from an equation. Parts e and f additionally require quadratic sign restrictions; this supports the secondary inequality mapping.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines the natural domain as all valid real inputs and Example 6 applies nonzero-denominator and non-negative-radicand conditions. Combine those conditions for square roots in denominators; factor the quadratic expressions to identify excluded values or allowed intervals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine denominator restrictions with square-root conditions, factor quadratics and distinguish strict from inclusive endpoints.

classification.difficultyReason: Transfer domain and range through square roots and reciprocals, distinguish excluded endpoints, and complete the square for two further radicands.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses domain and range with inclusive and exclusive bounds; algebraic domain restrictions and completing the square support those determinations.
questions.methodNote: Pages 7–8 define functions, domain and range and interval notation. Page 9 demonstrates reading a parabola's range and finding natural domains by excluding zero denominators and negative radicands. Apply these restrictions successively to square roots and reciprocals; complete the square to expose each further quadratic's bounds.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Transfer domain and range through square roots and reciprocals, distinguish excluded endpoints, and complete the square for two further radicands.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the positivity restriction on a logarithmic argument with a rational substitution, recognise squared binomial factors, and justify the logarithm power law on the original domain to prove the identity.

questions.mappingNote: Part b directly assesses evaluation at an algebraic argument; part a assesses the natural domain. The inspected section supplies the domain convention but does not demonstrate logarithm laws.
questions.methodNote: Use the natural-domain convention on page 9: retain inputs for which the formula is defined. Substitute the algebraic argument into the given function and simplify using factorisation and the logarithm power law.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine the positivity restriction on a logarithmic argument with a rational substitution, recognise squared binomial factors, and justify the logarithm power law on the original domain to prove the identity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Guided substitution establishes the intercepts and a second point before sketching a straight line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the specified intercept substitutions and x = 1 to sketch three lines through the origin.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b use two distinct intercepts. Part c uses the origin and one substituted point, matching the special-case method. Graphing a linear relationship is the most advanced directly assessed skill.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch three linear functions using two intercepts, or the origin and a second point when both intercepts coincide.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute each given coordinate pair into a linear equation and compare the resulting values.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct three pairs of linear graphs, read their intersections and confirm each result algebraically.

questions.methodNote: Page 15 gives the intercept method. Example 9 on page 16 plots two lines and reads their intersection; Example 10 confirms it by elimination and substitution.
